text: His commander has begged Nib for an ending before the Hush takes him too. Under the blade, Nib gives his word.
The voice is gone. Red floods back into the hole like a fever returning.
The knight leans in with all its weight and drives Nib down onto one knee.
Jaeha can't fight it, but Carry can move a summon's damage into his own body.
Half the knight's weight lands on Jaeha instead, and his nose bleeds again.
Nib feels the load ease and glances back, startled.
Yerin slides in with shaking, glowing hands. Whatever he gives away, she'll put back.
Through Link he borrows Nib's eyes and searches the empty helm for a flaw.
One thin crack in the rim, pulsing brighter than the rest.
Nib has spotted it as well. He refused to kill his commander. He won't refuse him an ending.
Jaeha's polite mask is gone. Nib won't do this alone. Jaeha will count him in.
The knight wrenches free for a last sweep. Jaeha watches the cracked shoulder. It always dips first.
On the count, Nib springs off the knight's forearm and drives both knives into the crack.
The knight sinks to its knees, beaten. The system admits what the red lamp knew: B-plus, registered as C.
Then the system prices Nib's commander: four hundred million won for his core. Or release.
To Yerin, a rookie on her first raid, it's a number from another world.
For a moment he's back at the rooftop room he shares with his sister Seoa, counting what they owe.
One tap would pay for all of it, and then some.
His finger hovers. Four years of trap-testing taught him to ask what a button does first.
Release means no money at all. It sends the knight home, core and all.
Nib asks for nothing. He stands before his commander, head bowed.
Jaeha looks past the money at Nib's back, and the choice makes itself.
He taps the button that pays nothing.
Nib spins round, wide-eyed. Nobody throws away a fortune for a goblin's sake.
Jaeha shrugs. A soldier belongs with his own people. Explaining that to Seoa will be harder.
The knight dissolves into rising light, its ash lifting like embers.
For one moment the helm holds a real face, old, scarred and kind. He knows what Nib found.
His last order gives the old rule a new meaning: Nib goes first so this man gets home.
Nib gives the Ninth Wall salute, fist on heart. Tears run below the mask. His voice holds.
Then the knight is gone, ash rising through the light. Nobody speaks.
The modern chains crumble to dust. All but one link.
Jaeha turns it to the light. Machined. Stamped with a mark. Monsters don't buy chains. People do.
The knight's sword stays behind: over two metres of dark iron with a nine-tower crossguard.
The Ninth Wall Blade slides into a slit in the air. It needs strength ninety. Jaeha has seven.
He draws it, and the weight slams it into the floor and drags him down too.
He heaves with a boot on the crossguard. Nothing. Nib reminds him whose sword it is. Yerin hides a laugh.
Pinned flat under his prize, Jaeha begs the system for a refund.
Then the rewards: two Operator levels, stronger Link and Carry, and something called Route Alignment at thirty percent.
Even a title. The trap rat is now, officially, The One Who Went Back.
His status holds a secret: his class is Operator, but others still see an F-rank summoner.
He has read that word all night and still has no idea what it means.
Nib's answer is perfectly accurate and no help at all.
A colder window: nobody can take this power from him, and if he's forced, it all shuts down.
No time to think. The gate closes in thirty seconds, and the hall is breaking into light.
Nib kicks the door Mok had bolted on them, and the bolt snaps.
Then he stands aside like a doorman and waves Jaeha out first, deadpan, as everything falls apart.
They sprint up the crumbling corridor with four seconds left. Nib runs last, watching their backs.
And they dive out into the subway pit as the gate snaps shut behind them.
On the street, at half past eleven, a crane lowers a rescue basket for whoever is left.
Choi Dongmin, thirty-four, Gate Rescue Corps, wraps Jaeha in foil and runs the numbers. They don't add up.
He points his cup at Nib, wrapped in foil like a tiny burrito. Jaeha's cover story is weak.
Nib sniffs the steaming cup like it's poisoned and suggests its owner try it first.
Choi freezes with the cup halfway down. Husks don't talk. Everyone knows that.
Jaeha switches on his customer-service smile, and Nib does his very best impression of a doll.
Then the billboard across the street lights up: Black Hound, live. Four dead, two missing, and the missing two are right here.
And there's Mok in a black suit, telling the story with the roles swapped. It's all the trap-tester's fault.
The man who had them locked in tells the cameras Jaeha is probably dead, his mouth not quite grave.
Yerin's hands fly to her mouth. Choi turns to the dead man on his bumper with some news.
The smile is gone. Mok has buried him on live television, so Jaeha knows where he's going next: his own funeral.
